```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A model reads a long document in pieces, called *chunks*, and chunking decides
what it can see together. A figure in one chunk and the sentence that explains
it in the next may never be read side by side. This guide covers the nine ways
harnessr cuts a document, the settings every one of them shares, and how to
compare chunkings before you pay for any reading.

Six of the nine segmenters make no model calls, and a seventh makes none by
default, so you can try them for nothing. `vignette("harnessr")` introduces the
package and the ideas used here, and `vignette("ingest")` covers the step before
this one.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")
```

`embedder = "lexical"` makes the one segmenter that embeds text, `semantic`, use
hashed bag-of-words vectors rather than an embeddings endpoint, so this guide
runs offline and gives the same chunks every time.

## What segmentation produces

`gr_segment()` takes a document from `gr_ingest()` (or anything `gr_ingest()`
accepts) and a segmentation, and returns a chunk set:

```{r}
doc <- gr_ingest(gr_example())
ch <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120))
ch
```

The segmentation can be a segmenter's name, a named list as above, or a
`gr_segment_spec()`. Each chunk records where it came from:

```{r}
ch$chunks[, c("chunk_id", "tokens", "page", "section", "block_id")]
```

`page` is `NA` here because the example is Markdown, which has no pages; a PDF
fills it in. `block_id` is `NA` on a chunk built from several blocks, and so is
`page` on a chunk that runs from one page onto the next. A chunk that is not
from one place says so rather than naming the first place it touches. This
provenance is what `ans$evidence` reports for every chunk an answer rests on.

You rarely call `gr_segment()` yourself. `answer_document()` does it, using the
`segment` part of a recipe:

```{r}
gr_recipe("survey")$segment[c("method", "max_tokens", "overlap_tokens")]
```

To change it, build a recipe of your own with
`gr_recipe(segment = list(...))`; `vignette("readers")` covers recipes.

## The nine segmenters

Each segmenter is a different hypothesis about where meaning breaks:

| segmenter | boundary hypothesis | cost | needs client | provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fixed` | meaning is uniform; cut on a ruler (the control condition) | free | no | none |
| `paragraph` | the author's paragraph breaks are real | free | no | page, section, block |
| `sentence` | sentences are atomic; pack tightly | free | no | page, section, block |
| `recursive` | use the strongest separator that still fits | free | no | none |
| `structural` | headings are boundaries; never merge across sections | free | no | page, section, block |
| `page` | the page is the unit: forms, invoices, scanned records | free | no | page, section, block |
| `semantic` | cut where consecutive embeddings diverge most | 1 embedding pass | yes | page, section, block |
| `contextual` | chunks prefixed with where they sit | free, or 1 call/chunk | only for `context_source = "llm"` | page, section, block |
| `proposition` | rewrite into standalone factual statements | 1 call per ~900-token batch | yes | none |

The cost and client columns come from the registry, so you can check them
rather than trust them:

```{r}
gr_segmenters()[, c("name", "cost", "needs_client", "calls")]
```

`paragraph` is the default. It packs the author's paragraphs, in order, into
chunks up to the cap. `sentence` packs sentences instead, which gives more,
smaller chunks with cleaner edges. `structural` never lets a chunk cross a
heading, and by default (`prefix_section = TRUE`) starts every chunk with its
section's heading, so the fourth chunk of a long "Methods" section still says it
is about methods. When the extractor found no sections, `structural` finds
headings itself: a Markdown `#` line, or a short line that is numbered or
written in capitals. `page` makes one chunk per page, splitting only a page too
long for the cap, and says so when it does.

`fixed` cuts the text into windows of equal size and ignores its structure,
which makes it the baseline to measure the others against. `recursive` splits on
the strongest separator that still gives pieces under the cap: by default blank
lines, then line breaks, then sentence ends, semicolons, commas and spaces. Set
your own cascade, strongest first, with `separators`.

`fixed` and `recursive` work on the whole document joined into one string, by
design, so their chunks carry no page or section. That is the cost of ignoring
structure, and it is reported as `NA` rather than guessed at:

```{r}
fx <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "fixed", max_tokens = 120))
fx$chunks[1:3, c("chunk_id", "page", "section", "block_id")]
```

The last three segmenters, `semantic`, `contextual` and `proposition`, are
covered below, under the settings and model calls they add.

## When a segmenter cannot run as asked

A segmenter that cannot do what was asked falls back to one that can, warns,
and records the change. `page` on a source with no page numbers falls back to
`paragraph`:

```{r warning = FALSE}
pg <- gr_segment(doc, "page")
pg$method
```

`semantic` without a client falls back to `paragraph`, and `proposition`
without one falls back to `sentence`. The fallback shows in `$method`
(`"semantic->paragraph"`, `"proposition->sentence"`) and in the `method` column
of `gr_chunk_stats()`, so a comparison never reports a chunking that did not
run. `contextual` keeps its name when `context_source = "llm"` has no client,
because only the source of its context lines changed; `$extra$context_source`
records `"metadata"`, the one that ran.

Every one of these warnings has the class `gr_segment_fallback`, and it is
carried onto the answer of any read that uses the chunks.

## Chunk size

`max_tokens` is the cap on a chunk's size, and every segmenter is held to it,
including one you register yourself. After a segmenter returns, `gr_segment()`
splits any chunk over the cap (at sentences, then words, then characters) and
counts how many it had to split in `$extra$cap_enforced`. The pieces keep the
page, section and block of the chunk they came from. If the active tokenizer
counts a single character as more than the cap, `gr_segment()` stops with an
error of class `gr_cap_unenforceable` rather than send a chunk the model will
reject.

A setting out of range is corrected and the correction is announced:

```{r}
tryCatch(gr_segment_spec("paragraph", max_tokens = 100, overlap_tokens = 500),
         warning = conditionMessage)
```

`max_tokens` is held to between 32 and 1,000,000, `overlap_tokens` to less than
`max_tokens`, and `min_tokens` to no more than `max_tokens`.

What the right size is depends on the reader. A reader that sends every chunk
pays for each request, so small chunks multiply the bill; one that picks the
best few chunks needs chunks small enough that the best few hold the answer and
little else. `vignette("readers")` compares them.

## Overlap

Without overlap, an answer that straddles a boundary is split between two
chunks and may be lost by both. `overlap_tokens` copies the end of each chunk
into the start of the next. It costs duplicated tokens, which
`gr_chunk_stats()` shows as a larger `total_tokens`:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 30, 60), function(ov)
  gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 120,
                                      overlap_tokens = ov)))))
```

The document is the same 534 tokens each time: at 60 tokens of overlap the
model would be sent 863, about 60% more. The carried text is cut at a sentence
boundary when one is close, otherwise at a word; text written without spaces
(Chinese, Japanese, Thai) is cut by characters. The overlap is trimmed so that
the chunk it opens still fits the cap.

Provenance counts the overlap. A chunk that opens with a sentence carried from
page 3 and goes on to page 4 reports page `NA`, since it is not wholly from
either.

Overlap applies to every segmenter except `page`, where the page is the unit,
and `proposition`, whose statements are written to stand alone, so its overlap
is always 0. `structural` applies it within a section, never across a heading.

## Minimum size

`min_tokens` merges a chunk smaller than this into the chunk before it, so a
one-line paragraph between two headings does not become a request of its own.
The merge happens only when the result still fits the cap. With a cap of 60
tokens the example's paragraphs give fourteen chunks, the smallest of 8 tokens;
`min_tokens = 30` folds one of them away:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 30), function(m)
  gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 60,
                                      min_tokens = m)))))
```

`fixed` and `page` ignore `min_tokens`. `structural` applies it within a
section only, because it never merges across headings: its 16-token first
chunk, the report's title, stays as it is whatever you set.

```{r}
gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                    min_tokens = 40)))
```

## Context lines

A chunk retrieved on its own can be hard to place: "it rose 17 percent" means
little without the section it came from. `contextual` packs paragraphs as
`paragraph` does, then starts each chunk with a bracketed line saying where it
sits. By default (`context_source = "metadata"`) the line is built from the
file name, section, page and position, for nothing:

```{r}
ctx <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "contextual", max_tokens = 120))
cat(ctx$chunks$text[2])
```

With `context_source = "llm"` a model writes the line instead, one call per
chunk, from the chunk and the document's first 1,500 tokens. The mock client below
stands in for that model:

```{r}
writer <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "This excerpt reports the 2024 results.")
ctx_llm <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "contextual", max_tokens = 120,
                                context_source = "llm"), client = writer)
cat(ctx_llm$chunks$text[2])
```

Room for the line is held back from each chunk before packing (90 tokens for
`"llm"`, the longest header the document could need for `"metadata"`, never
more than half of `max_tokens`), so adding the line never pushes a chunk over
the cap. A line that still does not fit is shortened; the document text is
not.

When a context call fails or is skipped at the run's limits, the chunk keeps
its text without a line. `$extra$blurbs_missing` counts those chunks, and a
`gr_segment_fallback` warning says so.

The context line is not the document's text, and a model may have written it.
So the chunk also keeps its body alone in a `source_text` column, and a
quotation from the chunk is checked against that, never against the line:

```{r}
ctx_llm$chunks$source_text[2]
```

## Segmenters that call a model

Three segmenters spend something, and each takes a `client`:

- `semantic` embeds the text a few sentences at a time (`semantic_window`,
  default 2) and cuts where two neighbouring windows differ most: at distances
  above the `semantic_percentile` (default 90; higher gives fewer, larger
  chunks). The packer then holds the pieces to the cap and the minimum.
- `contextual` with `context_source = "llm"` makes one call per chunk, as above.
- `proposition` sends the document in batches of about
  `proposition_batch_tokens` (default 900) and has the model rewrite each into
  standalone factual statements, with pronouns resolved and numbers kept as
  written. Its chunks are the model's words, so `source_text` holds the passage
  each was written from, and quotes are checked against that. A batch that
  cannot be rewritten is kept as written rather than dropped, with a warning,
  and counted in `$extra$batches_kept_as_written`.

```{r}
cl <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "unused")
sem <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "semantic", max_tokens = 120), client = cl)
gr_chunk_stats(sem)
sem$extra$embedding_source
```

`embedding_source` is `"lexical"` here, so the boundaries reflect shared words,
not meaning. With a real embeddings endpoint it is `"api"`.

These requests count against the run's limits, `gr_options(max_calls =,
max_cost_usd =)`, like any other. Called without a `trace`, `gr_segment()`
makes its own and returns it as `$trace`, so you can see what segmenting cost:

```{r}
gr_trace_summary(ctx_llm$trace)[, c("calls", "tokens_in", "tokens_out")]
```

`vignette("runs")` covers limits and traces.

## Comparing segmentations

`gr_chunk_stats()` sums a chunk set up in one row, so comparing chunkings is an
`rbind()`:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c("fixed", "paragraph", "sentence", "structural"),
  function(m) gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = m, max_tokens = 120)))))
```

`n` is the number of chunks, which is the number of requests for a reader that
sends every chunk. `total_tokens` grows with overlap and with text a segmenter
adds, such as the headings `structural` puts at the top of its chunks.
`over_cap` is 0 for anything `gr_segment()` returns, since the cap is enforced;
it is there for chunk sets built some other way. `method` names any fallback.

To compare what different chunkings do to an answer, give `gr_compare()`
recipes that differ only in their `segment`. It extracts the document once and
reuses a segmentation across recipes whose segment settings match, so only the
reading is paid for more than once:

```{r}
cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", list(
  gr_recipe("by_paragraph", segment = list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2)),
  gr_recipe("by_section", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2))), client = cl)
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "segmenter", "chunks", "reader", "chunks_used")]
```

## Previewing chunks in the Shiny app

The bundled app has a control for every segmentation setting: segmenter,
`max_tokens`, overlap and minimum chunk size. Its "Preview chunking" button shows
how the current settings cut the document before anything is spent on reading.
For a segmenter that calls a model, the button says so.

```{r eval = FALSE}
shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "harnessr"))
```

`GPTREAD_DOC_ROOTS` (colon-separated) sets which folders the app can read.
Unset, it defaults to `~/Documents`, falling back to your entire home directory,
so set it before exposing the app to anyone else. The app opens only the PDF,
Word, text, Markdown, HTML and image files under those folders, never hidden
files or hidden folders. `extract` and `screen` are not offered, since they read
against a protocol; use `gr_extract()` and `gr_screen()` (`vignette("review")`).
A blank cost cap leaves `gr_options("max_cost_usd")` in force rather than
lifting the limit.

## Your own segmenter

`gr_register_segmenter()` adds a segmenter that behaves like the built-ins: it
appears in `gr_segmenters()`, can be named in a recipe, and is held to the same
cap. `new_chunks()` builds the object it must return. `vignette("extending")`
has a worked example.

```{r include = FALSE}
gr_options(old)
```
